title: Year 8 Mathematics — Adding and Subtracting Fractions with Unlike Denominators
purpose: Team calibration vignette for Eduversal Subject Specialists. Specialists do not score an individual teacher's F2 — that is the school's own appraisers' instrument — but they do observe the same lessons during the two annual visits, and the School Appraisal Domain 2 rating is validated against what they see. Calibrating the team against a shared standard is what makes that validation defensible: a divergence between the school's aggregated Framework 2 picture and the Specialists' reading is only meaningful if the Specialists read consistently with each other. Working through the 45 F2 items is the exercise that builds that consistency.
usage_note: Participants read the full pack, score all 45 items independently without discussion, then the facilitator opens the distribution. Discussion time is spent only on items where the team spread is 2 or more.

teacher_profile.subject: Mathematics
teacher_profile.note_for_observers: Appraisal level is 'developing'. Items marked visible_from 'proficient' or 'lead' would normally be hidden for this teacher in a real appraisal. For calibration purposes we score all 45 so the team builds a shared reading of every item.

lesson_context.room: Maths Room 2 — fixed rows of double desks, whiteboard, projector, no visualiser
lesson_context.class_composition: Mixed attainment. 4 students on the school's EAL register, 2 students with individual learning plans (one dyslexia, one working two stages below), 3 students identified as high-attaining in the last EASE window.

artefact_1_lesson_plan.artefact_label: Artefact 1 — Ms. Rani's submitted lesson plan (reproduced as handed to the observer)

header.topic: Adding and subtracting fractions with unlike denominators
header.curriculum_reference: Written on the plan as: 'Stage 8 — Number — fractions'

stated_objectives: Students will understand how to add and subtract fractions with different denominators.
Students will be able to complete the worksheet on fraction addition.
artefact_1_lesson_plan.success_criteria: Not stated on the plan as a separate section. The plan contains the phrase 'students should get most of the worksheet right'.

planned_sequence.detail: Mental warm-up — simplify 6 fractions from the board.
Recap equivalent fractions from last lesson. Q&A.
Model two worked examples on the board: 1/2 + 1/3, then 3/4 − 2/5. Explain finding the common denominator.
Class works through 2 questions together on mini-whiteboards.
Worksheet — 12 questions, graded easy to hard.

differentiation_section.verbatim_text: Support: help weaker students during worksheet time. Extension: questions 11 and 12 are harder for the fast finishers.
differentiation_section.named_students: None named. No reference to the two individual learning plans or the EAL register.
differentiation_section.adapted_resources: None. One worksheet for all students.

grouping_and_modes.collaborative_work: Not planned. Guided practice is whole-class on mini-whiteboards, not paired or grouped.
grouping_and_modes.rationale_recorded: No rationale recorded for either mode.

materials_listed: Worksheet 'Fractions 3' — photocopied from the Year 8 scheme-of-work folder, origin not stated
Textbook p.84 — listed but not referenced anywhere else in the plan

strategies_present: Going over worksheet answers in the plenary (end)
formative_assessment_planned.note: Two checkpoints exist, but both are whole-class show-me formats. No individual check planned.

accessibility_notes.verbatim_text: Nothing recorded under a separate accessibility heading.
accessibility_notes.observable_in_plan: Worked examples use only numerical examples. No visual or area-model representation planned. No vocabulary list or sentence stems for the EAL students on the register.

cross_curricular_connections.verbatim_text: The plan contains a single line at the bottom: 'Link to recipes / real life if time.'
cross_curricular_connections.development: No further elaboration. No resource attached to support the connection.

artefact_1_lesson_plan.observer_note: This plan is genuine in structure and internally consistent, but light on differentiation, success criteria, and accessibility. Observers should score D1 items from this artefact alone — not from what Ms. Rani actually did in the room.

artefact_2_lesson_narrative.observer_position: Seated at the back-left corner. Able to see the board, most student faces, and circulate briefly during independent work.

timeline.note: Ms. Rani is in the room before the bell. Starter questions are already written on the board. Worksheets are stacked on the front desk in six piles. Projector is on and showing the lesson title.

Bell. Students enter over about 90 seconds. Ms. Rani stands at the door and greets students by name as they pass — she uses names for roughly two-thirds of the class, and says 'good morning' to the rest.
'Bags down, starter is on the board, you have four minutes.' Most students begin within 30 seconds. Three students at the back are still talking; Ms. Rani looks over but does not intervene yet.

Ms. Rani takes the register from her laptop at the front desk while students work. This takes about 70 seconds. She does not look up during it. The three back students remain off-task for this period.
One student (Dimas) arrives late. Ms. Rani says 'Dimas, starter's on the board, see me at break.' He sits and starts within 20 seconds. No further disruption. She marks him late on the laptop.

She moves from the desk and walks the middle aisle. Reaches the back trio; says quietly 'you've got two minutes left on this, show me three of them done.' They begin working. No raised voice, no whole-class callout.

'Right, pens down.' Takes about 20 seconds to get full attention. She goes through the six starter answers by asking for hands. Five students answer; four of them are from the front two rows. One student, Sari, answers twice.

Recap phase. 'Who remembers what we did with equivalent fractions last lesson?' Three hands. She takes the first one. Answer is partially correct — the student says 'you times the top and bottom by the same thing.' Ms. Rani says 'Good, yes — multiply numerator and denominator by the same number.' She restates it using the correct vocabulary and writes it on the board. She does not ask the student to expand or ask anyone else to build on it.

She writes the lesson objective on the board for the first time: 'To add and subtract fractions with different denominators.' She reads it aloud. No success criteria written. No student is asked to interpret it. It stays on the board for the rest of the lesson but is not returned to.

Teacher exposition begins. She works through 1/2 + 1/3 on the board. Her explanation is mathematically accurate and clearly sequenced: identify denominators, find lowest common multiple, convert both, add numerators, simplify. She uses correct terminology throughout — 'numerator', 'denominator', 'lowest common multiple', 'equivalent'.

Second worked example, 3/4 − 2/5. Same structure. Partway through she notices puzzled faces in the third row and says 'I'll do this step again — watch the bottom number.' She repeats the conversion step more slowly. This is unplanned and responsive.

Instruction is entirely in English. Two of the EAL students exchange a whispered explanation in Bahasa Indonesia; Ms. Rani notices, and allows it without comment. She does not offer any bilingual support herself, nor any vocabulary scaffold. No visual or area model is used at any point — the explanation is purely symbolic.

Guided practice. 'Mini-whiteboards out.' Distribution takes about 45 seconds — a student monitor hands them along the rows; the routine is clearly established and students know their part. She poses 2/3 + 1/4. 'Show me when you've got it.'

About 20 of 26 boards go up. She scans them quickly from the front. 'Good — I can see most of you have 11/12. A few of you have 3/7 — that's adding the tops and the bottoms, which is the trap. Look again.' She addresses the misconception to the whole class, does not name individuals, and does not follow up with the six students whose boards did not go up.
Second whiteboard question, 5/6 − 1/2. Roughly 22 boards up, most correct. She says 'much better' and moves on. No third check.

Transition to independent work. 'Worksheets coming round — start at question one, you've got fifteen minutes.' Worksheet distribution takes about 80 seconds because she hands them out herself row by row. Some students at the back wait with nothing to do for around a minute.

Students working. Noise level is low and task-focused. Ms. Rani circulates the left half of the room, stopping at four students. Her interactions are specific: to one student she says 'you've found the common denominator but you've only changed the first fraction — what about the second one?' The student corrects it themselves.

She has circulated the left and centre. She does not reach the right-hand column of desks at any point during the lesson. Two students there have their hands up briefly and put them down again after about 40 seconds; one of them stops working and starts drawing in the margin. This is not noticed.

One of the high-attaining students finishes the worksheet including questions 11 and 12. She raises her hand. Ms. Rani says 'well done — check them again carefully.' No extension task is provided. The student re-checks for about a minute, then sits quietly for the remaining time.

A student asks, unprompted, 'Miss, why do they have to be the same on the bottom?' Ms. Rani answers: 'Because you can only add pieces that are the same size — thirds and halves aren't the same size.' Accurate and well-pitched. She does not open the question to the class or build on it, and returns to circulating.
'Two minutes, finish the one you're on.' She returns to the front.

Plenary. She reads out answers to questions 1 to 6 while students mark their own. Students call out corrections. She does not collect data on how many got them right, does not revisit the objective on the board, and does not ask what students found difficult.
'Finish the rest for homework, hand it in Thursday.' Bell. Students pack up and leave in an orderly way. Whiteboards are collected by the monitor without prompting.
Lesson ends. Total teaching time used: approximately 43 of the 45 minutes. Ms. Rani stays to speak with Dimas about his lateness.

artefact_2_lesson_narrative.observer_note: Interpersonal climate throughout was calm and respectful. No student was spoken to sharply at any point. No behaviour incident escalated. The right-hand column of the room received no teacher contact during independent work.

artefact_3_assessment_appendix.artefact_label: Artefact 3 — Assessment evidence supplied after the lesson

items.label: The worksheet used in the lesson ('Fractions 3')
items.detail: 12 questions. Q1–6 are unlike-denominator additions with small numbers. Q7–10 involve subtraction. Q11–12 are two-step word problems. The worksheet carries no marking criteria, no marks-per-question, and no statement of what a good answer looks like. The header is the photocopied original from the scheme folder and still carries another school's logo.

items.label: Assessment criteria shown to students
items.detail: None displayed in the lesson and none printed on the worksheet. When asked afterwards, Ms. Rani says 'they know they need to show the common denominator step — I always tell them.' It was not stated aloud during this lesson.

items.label: Cognitive level of the task
items.detail: Q1–10 are procedural application, appropriate to Stage 8. Q11–12 require selecting the operation from a context, which is a reasonable stretch. Nothing in the task is designed to surface misconceptions specifically — the 3/7 error seen on the whiteboards would simply appear as a wrong answer, not as diagnostic information.

items.label: Edunav records — spot check
items.detail: Ms. Rani's Year 8B mark record shows the last three assessments entered. The most recent (a Week 1 baseline quiz) was entered 9 school days after it was sat. The two before it were entered within 3 days. One student's Week 1 score is blank with no note explaining the absence. Entries are otherwise accurate and interpretable.

items.label: Marked books — sample of six exercise books
items.detail: Work is marked up to two weeks ago. Marking is predominantly ticks and crosses with a score out of 10 at the end of each exercise. Three of the six books contain a written comment; all three read 'Good work' or 'Take more care'. One book contains a specific comment: 'You are finding the common denominator correctly but forgetting to convert the second fraction — try questions 3 and 5 again.' That student has attempted the two questions again below the comment. No book shows a next-step target that the student could act on without further explanation. There is no evidence of student self-assessment or peer marking in any book.

items.label: Student-facing criteria and self-assessment
items.detail: No self-assessment or peer-assessment structure is present in the books or in the lesson. Students mark their own answers right/wrong in the plenary but are not asked to judge the quality of their method against any criterion. When asked whether students could self-assess using criteria, Ms. Rani says 'they'd just tick everything right.'

items.label: Progress monitoring evidence
items.detail: She keeps a printed class list with ticks and crosses per topic, updated most weeks. When asked, she can name three students who are struggling with fractions and describes what she has noticed about each. She could not describe the trajectory of the class as a whole, and did not reference any EASE data.

items.label: Action taken after the last assessment
items.detail: After the Week 1 baseline she re-taught simplifying fractions to the whole class for one lesson, because 'a lot of them got question 4 wrong'. There is no record of which students needed it, and the re-teach was not differentiated. No enrichment was provided for those who had already mastered it. Her Week 2 plan shows the re-teach was added; nothing else changed.

artefact_4_values_and_curriculum_notes.artefact_label: Artefact 4 — Supplementary notes for items requiring wider context

notes.detail: The lesson plan references 'Stage 8 — Number — fractions' but does not cite a specific curriculum objective code. All content taught is traceable to Stage 8 Number. Ms. Rani did not tell students how this lesson sits in the wider sequence, beyond referring back to the previous lesson.

No explicit values reference was made during the lesson. Ms. Rani modelled patience and respect consistently in her interactions, particularly with the late-arriving student and the student who asked the 'why' question. There was no contrived or bolted-on values moment, and equally no authentic one arising from the content.

notes.topic: Persistence with struggling students (relevant to D3.21)
notes.detail: In a follow-up conversation Ms. Rani names two students she is worried about and describes what she has tried: moving one to the front, and speaking to the student's form tutor. She has not contacted parents and has not spoken to the SEN coordinator about the student on the dyslexia plan. She says 'I keep meaning to but the term got busy.'

notes.topic: Knowledge of individual performance patterns (relevant to D3.6)
notes.detail: Seating is alphabetical, not by attainment or need. The student working two stages below is seated in the right-hand column, which received no teacher contact during independent work. During the lesson Ms. Rani made one in-the-moment adjustment (repeating the conversion step at 10:30) but it was triggered by facial expressions in the room rather than by knowledge of specific students. She did not direct any support to the two students on individual learning plans, and did not reference any student's prior performance in her decisions during the 45 minutes. In the follow-up conversation she can name three students struggling with fractions without consulting records.

See Artefact 3, marked books. In-lesson verbal feedback was specific and actionable on the four students she reached (for example the common-denominator correction at 10:42). Written feedback in books is predominantly non-specific. The two channels differ markedly in quality, which is the tension observers must resolve when scoring this item.

Every explanation given during the lesson was mathematically accurate. Terminology was used correctly and consistently. No misconception was introduced by the teacher. Her answer to the unprompted 'why' question was conceptually sound rather than merely procedural.

notes.topic: Interdisciplinary connection (relevant to D1.10 and lesson delivery)
notes.detail: The 'link to recipes / real life if time' line in the plan was never used in the lesson. No cross-curricular or real-world connection was made at any point during the 45 minutes.

notes.topic: Higher-order thinking (relevant to D3.5 and D3.10)
notes.detail: Across the whole lesson, every teacher-initiated question was recall or procedural. The single conceptual question in the room came from a student, not the teacher. No task required analysis, evaluation, or creation — Q11–12 on the worksheet require selecting an operation from context, which is the highest cognitive demand present, and only three students reached them.

notes.topic: Distribution of response opportunities (relevant to D3.11)
notes.detail: Across the lesson, 9 distinct students spoke aloud out of 26. Ms. Rani used hands-up exclusively; no cold-calling, no think-pair-share, no randomiser. Sari answered twice. No student from the right-hand column spoke at any point.

Two distinct strategies are observable: teacher-led worked-example exposition, and whole-class mini-whiteboard checking. Independent worksheet practice is a third if counted as a strategy. No collaborative, discussion-based, visual/manipulative, or inquiry strategy was used.

recommended_flow: Distribute the pack. Give the team 15 minutes to read all four artefacts before any scoring.
Score all 45 items independently. No discussion, no looking at neighbours' screens. Budget 25–30 minutes.
Open the distribution. Do not discuss items where the team already agrees.
Work only the items with a spread of 2 or more. Ask the highest and lowest scorer to each state their evidence before anyone argues.
Record an anchor decision for every item discussed: the agreed score and the one-sentence reason. This is the artefact you keep.
expected_spread_hotspots: D1.4 — the plan has a differentiation line but names no students; teams typically split 1 vs 2.
D2.1 — she misses the right-hand column entirely but handles the back trio well; splits 2 vs 3.
D2.8 — register is accurate but taken while three students are off-task; splits 2 vs 3.
D3.3 — objective is written and read aloud but never revisited and no success criteria; splits 2 vs 3.
D3.13 — a clear I-do/We-do/You-do sequence exists, but release happens with six students unchecked; splits 2 vs 3.
D3.16 — nothing explicit, but consistent modelling; teams split hard on whether absence of a values moment is a 2 or whether modelling alone earns 3.
D3.19 — two genuine checkpoints, but no individual checks and no follow-up on the six blank boards; splits 2 vs 3.
D4.4 — one entry at 9 days against a 5-day indicator, others fine; splits 2 vs 3.
facilitator_reminders: The 1–4 descriptors in the framework are the only authority. If two people disagree, both should read the level-2 and level-3 descriptor aloud before arguing.
Resist the urge to score the teacher generously because she is likeable in the narrative. The question is what the descriptor says, not whether she had a good day.
Equally, resist scoring harshly to look rigorous. A 3 means 'Proficient' — it is the expected standard, not a compliment.
